title: Do Not Make Me Guess
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 6 of 40
content:
In the morning, Greg made coffee as though nothing in the world had changed.

The coffee maker made a noise like an angry lawn mower, and Greg slapped the side of it with the affectionate impatience of a man who had kept cheap equipment working for years.

“Morning, you beautiful disaster,” he told the machine.

“Are you talking to it or me?”

“Both. One of you owes me a new filter.”

The joke landed, but there was something underneath it. Last night had happened. I could still feel the impression of his hand at my waist, the almost unbearable tenderness of being wanted without being hurried. In daylight, my borrowed sweatpants on his legs looked ridiculous, and I was suddenly afraid that our happiness would collapse under the weight of ordinary breakfast.

Greg saw me looking at the clothes.

“Just so we're clear, I'm returning these,” he said. “Unless you wanna start a collection of very fashionable ankle pants.”

“Keep them.”

He set the mug down. “Hey. Did you just give me your only comfortable sweatpants because you think I need a souvenir?”

I hesitated.

“Okay,” he said, softer. “Then let's not make that the rule. I'll bring them back after I wash them.”

He leaned against the counter rather than approaching me. It gave me space to laugh, to look at him, to decide what I wanted to do. I crossed the kitchen and caught his ridiculous shirt in my fingers.

“Can I kiss you before the machine kills us both?”

“Please. I need something to remember me by.”

His mouth was warm with coffee, and he laughed when I nearly knocked over the sugar jar. The second kiss was less graceful. I liked it better.

He stood in my kitchenette wearing the same T-shirt from yesterday and a pair of borrowed sweatpants that were too short in the legs. His hair was sleep-tousled. One hand held a mug; the other tried to operate the ancient coffee maker without making eye contact with the machine.

“It’s judging me,” he said.

I was still in bed, wrapped in the blankets that had seemed perfectly ordinary before the night became something else. “It knows what you did.”

Greg looked over his shoulder. “I made coffee.”

“That’s not what I meant.”

“Oh.” His ears turned pink. “Right.”

The night returned in fragments: the careful questions, my yes, the way Greg had kissed me as if there were nowhere else he needed to be. There had been laughter, warmth, and an afternoon that ended with the two of us tangled in blankets while the bakery below prepared for the next day.

Nothing about it had felt rushed. Nothing had felt taken.

Still, morning had a way of making every decision look larger.

Greg carried two mugs to the bed and sat on the edge, leaving enough room for me to decide whether to close it. I accepted mine. The coffee was sweet and slightly too strong.

“I’m sorry,” he said.

I blinked. “For the coffee?”

“No.” He looked at the mug. “For not asking whether you wanted me to stay.”

I held the coffee between both hands. “You didn’t have to ask.”

“I know. But I should have.”

The admission was disarming. I had expected him to be cheerful, maybe embarrassed, perhaps distant. I had not expected him to offer an apology before I knew me needed one.

“I wanted you to stay,” I said.

Greg looked up.

“I still want you here,” I continued. “I just don’t know what this is supposed to look like.”

“Neither do I.”

“You seem like somebody who would know.”

“I look very confident from a distance.”

“That’s because your hair has authority.”

He smiled, then sobered. “We can decide one piece at a time.”

“What piece are we deciding now?”

“Whether you want breakfast.”

The question made me laugh. Greg looked pleased, but he did not use the moment to avoid the larger conversation.

“Yes,” I said. “I want breakfast.”

“Great. I can make pancakes.”

“Do you know how?”

“I know several shapes.”

He got up. The room felt different when he moved away, emptier in a way that was not yet painful but could become so if I stared at it.

“Greg.”

He turned.

“Are you going to disappear?”

The question came out smaller than I intended.

He set the mug down. “No.”

“You don’t know that.”

“I know what I’m choosing.”

“People choose things and then change their minds.”

“They do.”

“You might.”

“I might.” He walked back to the bed and crouched so I was looking at each other. “If I change my mind, I’ll tell you. I won’t punish you with silence and call it kindness.”

My chest tightened.

“And if you change yours,” he said, “you tell me. You don’t have to stay because we kissed. You don’t owe me a relationship because I bought a chair.”

“The chair was very nice.”

“It was.”

“I might owe you a little.”

“A cinnamon roll would settle the debt.”

The tension loosened enough for me to breathe.

Greg stood again and began making pancakes. He hummed while he worked, the melody slipping in and out of tune. I watched his shoulders move beneath the shirt, the easy confidence of his hands, the way he checked the pan before adding batter.

The pancake in the middle of the pan had acquired a shape that looked remarkably like a badly tuned guitar.

"That's either breakfast or my first album cover," Greg said.

"Your first album cover?"

"Less flattering. Worse lighting."

He slid the pancake onto a plate, shook his head at its uneven edges, and pushed the best one toward me. I took the crooked one instead. It tasted of cinnamon and something he had almost certainly put in without measuring.

"Hey," he said after a minute. "We should talk about what last night means before I accidentally start acting like I know."

I set down my fork. "That's a good idea."

"Okay. For starters, you don't owe me a whole future because we had a good night."

"I know." The words were easy to say and less easy to believe. "And I want to be clear that I'm ethically non-monogamous. I prefer polyamory. I'm not asking you to share every part of your life with anybody else, but I won't pretend I only ever love one person."

Greg nodded slowly. "Thanks for telling me straight. I might have questions. Maybe some really dumb ones."

"Ask."

"Does this mean I can still make you awful pancakes without taking a ticket and getting in line?"

I laughed hard enough to choke on my coffee. "Yes, Greg."

"Great. I have a competitive advantage in awful pancakes."

He reached for my hand across the table and waited for me to meet him halfway. I did. We hadn't made a schedule or promised the world, but we had decided neither one of us would have to guess what the other meant by wanting to see them again.

“You’re staring,” he said without turning.

“You’re making breakfast in my kitchen.”

“That’s not a defense.”

“It’s my best one.”

“I accept.”

The first pancake was too pale. The second was shaped vaguely like a crescent moon. The third landed halfway on the plate.

“You said several shapes,” I reminded him.

“I didn’t say they were edible shapes.”

I ate all three.

After breakfast, Greg washed the dishes. He did not put my things away without asking. When he picked up a mug, he paused and looked at me.

“Cabinet or counter?”

“Counter.”

“Good to know.”

The tiny question touched me more than it should have. I had lived with people who moved through my space as if my preferences were clutter. Greg treated a mug like a negotiation.

When he finished, he dried his hands on a towel and faced me.

“There’s something I want to say.”

“That sounds serious.”

“It is, but not bad serious.”

He leaned against the counter. “I’m attracted to you. I like you. I like what happened yesterday, and I would like it to happen again. But I don’t want you to feel like you have to be easy for me. You can ask for space. You can say no. You can change the plan halfway through.”

“You’re giving me a lot of instructions for someone who just burned a pancake.”

“I contain contradictions.”

“So do I.”

“I know.”

The warmth returned to his eyes.

I stepped closer. “What if I don’t know what I want until I’m already doing it?”

“Then we check in while we’re doing it.”

“What if I say yes and then panic?”

“Then we stop and panic together, or separately, depending on what you want.”

“What if I don’t say anything?”

“Then I ask.”

I was close enough now to smell coffee and clean soap. Greg did not reach for me.

“What if I want you to kiss me?”

“Then you can tell me.”

“You could ask.”

His smile was gentle. “Do you want me to?”

“Yes.”

“Can I kiss you?”

“Yes.”

The kiss was not like yesterday. It did not carry the nervous rush of a first crossing. It was slower, more knowing. Greg's hand settled at my waist only after I touched his shoulder. When I leaned back against the counter, he followed without pressing me there.

“Still okay?” he whispered.

“Yes.”

“Tell me if that changes.”

“I will.”

He kissed the corner of my mouth. Then my cheek. Then the place beneath my ear that made my breath catch.

“Still okay?”

I pulled him closer by the front of his shirt. “Ask me one more time and I’m going to start charging you for repetition.”

“I can pay in muffins.”

“Then continue.”

The morning unfolded in a softer rhythm. There were kisses and laughter, hands resting where they were welcome, and a moment when Greg's forehead pressed against mine while both of us tried to remember how breathing worked.

We kept the morning soft with kisses, laughter, and a long conversation about what each of us wanted next.

Later, after we had talked ourselves tired, I woke from a nap with Greg asleep beside me. His arm lay across the mattress, not holding me, only near enough that I could reach it. Sunlight moved across the wall.

I had expected regret. Instead, I felt the quiet shock of being safe after wanting something.

Greg woke when I shifted. “Hey.”

“Hey.”

“Did I talk in my sleep?”

“You apologized to the pancakes.”

“They were under a lot of pressure.”

I turned toward him. “What happens now?”

He looked at the ceiling. “We keep talking. We keep asking. We see if we like each other when we’re tired and annoying.”

“You’re already annoying.”

“Excellent. We’re ahead of schedule.”

I smiled, but the question remained.

“Do you want to call this dating?” I asked.

Greg considered me. “Do you?”

“I don’t know.”

“That’s okay.”

“You’re not going to make me guess?”

“No.” He touched the back of my hand. “I want to date you. If you want to date me. If you don’t, I still want to be someone you can call. But I’m not going to pretend I only want friendship if that isn’t true.”

His directness made my heart beat harder.

“I want to date you,” I said.

“Okay.”

“That’s all?”

“I’m trying to remain calm.”

“You’re failing.”

“I’m doing my best.”

He kissed my hand. The gesture was almost old-fashioned, and yet it felt less like a performance than a promise to keep showing up.

That evening, I walked with him to the boardwalk. Greg carried the new chair. I carried the guitar case. The division of weight was not equal, but it was agreed upon. When I reached the sea wall, he set the chair down and waited for me to sit before taking the space beside me.

“I’m going to write a song about this,” he said.

“About the chair?”

“About the way you keep making me ask.”

“That sounds threatening.”

“It’s affectionate.”

The sunset spread pink and orange across the water. Greg's shoulder rested against mine.

“You know,” I said, “you can tell me what you want too.”

He looked at me.

“You keep making space for me,” I continued. “But you’re allowed to take up some.”

The expression on his face was so tender that I nearly looked away.

“I want to,” he said.

“Then do.”

Greg shifted closer. His hand found mine between the chairs.

“I want to be here,” he said. “With you. I want to learn what your good days look like. I want to make breakfast badly and hear you complain about my furniture. I want to know whether you ever stop looking at exits.”

“Do you want the honest answer?”

“Always.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll sit where you can see the door.”

I squeezed his hand.

The ocean did not promise anything. The future remained uncertain. But Greg was beside me, asking instead of assuming, making room instead of taking it.

For that evening, it was enough.
